articles.title: Walmart, e.l.f. Beauty use tariff refunds to cut prices in 2026
articles.summary: Walmart, e.l.f. Beauty, and Tractor Supply are among companies directing billions in refunds toward lower prices rather than profits
articles.body:
Major retailers and consumer goods companies are directing tariff refund payments toward price cuts as inflation-fatigued shoppers pull back on spending, according to The Wall Street Journal. The refunds trace back to a Supreme Court decision earlier this year holding that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not give President Donald Trump authority to impose those tariffs, an outcome that set off more than $160 billion in payments back to importers.

Walmart said it rolled back prices on 11,000 items, including ground beef, using roughly $2.9 billion in tariff refunds. Chief Financial Officer John David Rainey said on an earnings call that shoppers began making visible spending trade-offs in June as gas prices climbed above $4 a gallon. The company said the price impact for consumers would be felt in the current fiscal third quarter .

E.l.f. Beauty, which received about $50 million in refunded tariff payments, ran a series of pricing tests before permanently lowering prices across around 10% of its catalog, among them its Cream Glide Lip Liner. Fields explained that the initial test involved dropping the Halo Glow Skin Tint's price by $4, a move that drove unit sales up by close to 40%. Net sales for the quarter ended June 30 climbed 36% to $479.4 million, the company said.

Tractor Supply has channeled its refunds into shielding customers from freight and fuel cost increases, lowering prices on products including pine shavings and premium pet food rather than pushing those expenses onto shoppers, according to the Wall Street Journal. Chief Financial Officer Kurt Barton declined to disclose the refund amount the company received. Tractor Supply's gross margin edged up to 37.1% for the quarter ending June 27 from 36.9% in the same period last year, though the company anticipates that freight costs will weigh on margins during the back half of the year once refund benefits diminish.

Not every retailer is passing refunds to shoppers. Lowe's CEO Marvin Ellison told CNBC that the company received roughly $80 million in refunds and chose to direct them toward shareholder returns rather than price reductions. Kohl's CEO Michael Bender told CNBC the company put $100 million of its refunds into its gross margin and plans to invest the remainder in deeper inventory.

According to CNBC, AlixPartners managing director Bryan Eshelman, who leads the firm's retail practice, said the tariff refund situation is more complicated than simply deciding how to spend the money. Tariff expenses were typically absorbed into broader cost structures rather than assigned to specific products, making it nearly impossible to determine what share of any refund corresponds to the extra amount a given consumer paid. "How does a consumer know that the price went down commensurate with the level of rebate?" Eshelman said.

Burlington Stores said it plans to reinvest all $55 million of its tariff refunds into lower prices for shoppers over the second half of its fiscal year. Chief Executive Michael O'Sullivan said the company intends to use the refunds to improve the deals it already offers customers.

articles.title: Justiça decreta prisão de suspeito de agredir médica e idosa em SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Mandado de prisão foi expedido na segunda-feira (31), pela Justiça de Santa Fé do Sul. Médica, que teve os dentes quebrados, deixou a UTI e foi para o quarto. Mulher de 62 anos aguarda cirurgia após fraturar o joelho ao ser atropelada.
articles.summary: A Justiça de Santa Fé do Sul decretou a prisão de João Carlos Romero, suspeito de agredir uma médica e atropelar uma idosa de 62 anos durante a fuga.
articles.body:
A Justiça de Santa Fé do Sul (SP) decretou a prisão preventiva de João Carlos Romero, 23 anos, suspeito de espancar a namorada, uma médica de 25 anos, e fugir do local de carro, atropelando uma mulher de 62 anos que estava na calçada . A fuga do suspeito foi registrada por câmeras de segurança (veja o vídeo) . O mandado foi expedido na segunda-feira (31) pelo Tribunal de Justiça de São Paulo (TJ-SP). Ele é considerado foragido pela Polícia Civil.

Segundo o advogado da médica, Carlos da Silva Júnior, a vítima deixou a Unidade de Terapia Intensiva (UTI) e foi transferida para um quarto do hospital . Ela havia sido internada após sofrer agressões com socos, chutes e empurrões, na noite de sábado (29). A vítima teve os dentes quebrados e o rosto deformado , segundo o advogado.

De acordo com o registro policial, a mulher teve ferimentos no rosto, sangramento na orelha, hematomas e sinais de enforcamento.

Mulher de 62 anos, atropelada por carro de suspeito em fuga, sofreu fratura no joelho; homem teve a prisão decretada por espancar a namorada em Santa Fé do Sul (SP) — Foto: Fotos: Arquivo pessoal

Durante a fuga, o suspeito ainda atropelou uma mulher de 62 anos que estava na calçada, por volta das 18h30. Câmeras de segurança de imóveis registraram o momento da fuga (assista acima) . Segundo familiares, a mulher procurava um gato no momento em que foi atingida. A idosa sofreu fratura no joelho e deverá passar por cirurgia nos próximos dias .

De acordo com o filho dela, o acidente ocorreu depois que o carro perdeu o controle ao passar sobre um bueiro destampado no meio da via . O veículo teria avançado sobre a calçada e atingido a mulher.

A mulher está em casa, acamada e com dores pelo corpo, segundo o filho. A cirurgia está prevista para a sexta-feira (4), em Santa Fé.

Câmeras de segurança registraram veículo de suspeito em fuga, após namorada ser espancada em Santa Fé do Sul (SP), no sábado (29): idosa foi atropelada — Foto: Fotos: Câmeras de segurança

O mandado de prisão preventiva contra Romero foi assinado pelo juiz Rafael Almeida Moreira de Souza, da 3ª Vara Cumulativa de Santa Fé do Sul, nesta segunda-feira (31). A decisão cita os artigos 312 e 313 do Código de Processo Penal e determina a prisão para garantia da ordem pública e para assegurar a aplicação da lei penal.

O documento também registra como enquadramentos penais os artigos 147 e 129, parágrafo 13, do Código Penal, referentes, respectivamente, ao crime de ameaça e à lesão corporal praticada contra a mulher por razões da condição do sexo feminino.

Além da prisão, a Justiça concedeu à médica medidas protetivas de urgência , determinando a proibição de aproximação e de contato do investigado com a vítima, inclusive por meio de terceiros. Segundo a decisão, as medidas devem continuar valendo mesmo em caso de eventual soltura ou revogação da prisão preventiva.

A decisão também determina que a investigação policial prossiga, incluindo a realização de depoimentos de testemunhas que ainda não foram formalmente ouvidas.

João Carlos Romero é considerado foragido. O veículo usado na fuga foi localizado ainda na segunda-feira, na área rural de Santana da Ponte Pensa, apurou a TV TEM .

João Carlos Romero é suspeito de espancar companheira em Santa Fé do Sul (SP) e atropelar mulher de 62 anos durante a fuga; Justiça decretou sua prisão — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram

O caso começou na noite de sábado (29), quando a médica estava na casa do namorado, no bairro Jardim Europa II, em Santa Fé do Sul. Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, ela relatou à polícia que foi agredida após uma discussão, quando tentou atender a uma ligação da mãe.

A mulher conseguiu deixar o imóvel e pedir ajuda aos vizinhos. A equipe policial foi acionada e encontrou a vítima sendo atendida pelo Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu).

Inicialmente, ela foi levada para a Santa Casa de Santa Fé do Sul. Devido à gravidade dos ferimentos, foi transferida para a Beneficência Portuguesa de São José do Rio Preto , onde permaneceu internada.

Segundo o advogado, as agressões teriam ocorrido durante uma crise de ciúmes do suspeito . A médica também pediu medidas protetivas de urgência. Após a agressão, Romero fugiu.

articles.title: The Movement: Meta settlement gets praise, pushback from the right
articles.summary: Family- and culture-focused groups on the right praised last week’s court settlement that requires Meta to institute safety and addiction guardrails for teenagers on its platforms. But free speech and innovation advocates are less than thrilled, as the settlement represents the biggest victory yet for a novel legal strategy that avoids First Amendment concerns. The settlement lands…
articles.body:
Family- and culture-focused groups on the right praised last week’s court settlement that requires Meta to institute safety and addiction guardrails for teenagers on its platforms.

But free speech and innovation advocates are less than thrilled, as the settlement represents the biggest victory yet for a novel legal strategy that avoids First Amendment concerns.

The settlement lands amid a broader tech backlash, particularly to artificial intelligence and the data centers required for its proliferation, and as the debate heats up among conservatives over how to balance the GOP’s traditional focus on anti-regulation and free speech, protections for young people, and parental rights.

Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, last week agreed to a $17 billion settlement with 47 attorneys general that had brought claims against the company alleging it designed its products with addictive algorithms intentionally to hook children and teenagers, and collected data on children without parental consent. The money will be paid out to the states in different amounts over the next decade.

But the result is hardly about the money — Meta also agreed to adopt changes to Facebook and Instagram for teenagers to minimize the worst effects of social media, including allowing users to disable endless scrolling, imposing two-hour time limits that only a parent can disable, silencing notifications during school hours and hiding the count of “likes.”

Pro-family conservatives have been clamoring for such controls for years. Michael Toscano , director of the Family First Technology Institute at the Institute for Family Studies , said in a statement that he still wants more layers of age verification for social media and app stores, but that the guardrails in the settlement are a positive step.

“Meta deserves no kudos for this action, but we should not forget that many other social media platforms are harming children, as well,” said Toscano. “This is a huge win for America’s children and families, and the mass movement that helped produce this result deserves our thanks.”

Melissa Henson , media and culture policy expert at Concerned Women for America , said she was surprised by the settlement, since Meta had gone all the way in court in previous trials. The guardrails in the settlement are along the same lines as what advocates have been pressing for, Henson said.

“I think it indicates that there has been an ability, just not a willingness, to implement these changes all along,” Henson said. “But I also acknowledge that Meta acting alone in isolation, as big as Facebook is and as big as Instagram is, Meta acting alone is not going to change the social media ecosystem.”

Tim Chapman , president of Advancing American Freedom , praised the settlement on social platform X and urged other social media companies to take the same steps.

“There is plenty to like in this settlement,” Chapman said. “If you are a parent of teenagers you understand the addictive nature of social media apps targeted at our kids. Meta, through their action, is now acknowledging that as well.”

But there are detractors, including those who would prefer tech safety be enforced by parents, not the government, and pro-business types who worry about setting a precedent for over-regulation if the settlement guidelines turn into federal statutes.

Neeraja Deshpande, a policy analyst at the Independent Women’s Forum , said she’s not thrilled about the power this settlement, and any subsequent legislation, gives to the government or the tech companies over something that should be a social contract in communities and families.

“I do think we’re outsourcing parenting and child-rearing to big tech companies,” Deshpande said. “So it’s like when we put the burden on the tech companies, when we say, ‘Oh, it’s the tech companies’ fault for building this addictive algorithm and like doing marketing to kids or whatever,’ I just, I don’t buy it. I think it’s ultimately the parents’ responsibility.”

The tide has turned against tech in many forms with the general public quite recently, as the proliferation of AI and the high-profile spread of data centers around the U.S. provide tangible scapegoats for Americans’ anxieties about unemployment and high costs of living.

Conservatives have traditionally been the party of less regulation and more speech rights but are now somewhat divided between those on the “tech right,” who seek to keep the juice of innovation flowing in America’s favor — and, on social media, keep unfettered access to online speech — and the “tech temperance” coalition, who are calling for regulation to reverse the social and cultural ills of social media and artificial intelligence.

The former group includes First Amendment advocates who see the Meta settlement as an end-run around a negotiated piece of legislation or a thorough judicial process in public view.

“This is the latest example of the newest legal strategy, which is, ‘Okay, we’re not going to go after the content of this stuff being addictive because that content is protected by Section 230, that liability protection. We’re gonna say it’s the design features that are addicting,’” said Jessica Melugin , director of the Center for Technology and Innovation at the Competitive Enterprise Institute .

“Now, I don’t buy that, because if you switch out the content, so one example that’s given often is, what if all the content on this platform was videos of paint drying? Would people be addicted to it, even with autoplay and infinite scroll?”

The role of parents is also hotly debated. Melugin said parents have the right to not buy their kids a smartphone or impose more controls that already exist. Henson, on the other hand, noted many parents struggle to figure out what controls are available and how to turn them on or off, so further attempts to regulate should start by making the most-restrictive settings default.

“Parents shouldn’t have to take a master’s course in social media in order to learn how to set up the parental controls,” Henson said.

The next step, Henson and others say, is for Congress to move forward on legislation like the bipartisan Kids’ Online Safety Act that would enact protections on social media platforms for those under 17.

Welcome to The Movement , a weekly newsletter looking at the influences and debates on the right in Washington. I’m Helen Huiskes, Senate reporter. Happy September!

Send me tips, comments, and suggestions: hhuiskes@thehill.com

GOP REPORT ADDS FUEL TO PUSH FOR ABORTION PILL CRACKDOWN

Anti-abortion groups see a promising future for further regulation of the abortion pill mifepristone as lawmakers and President Trump seek to limit its availability and use.

Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, released a report last week detailing the results of an investigation the panel launched into the safety practices of mifepristone manufacturers. Republican Sens. James Lankford (Okla.), Steve Daines (Mont.) and Cindy Hyde-Smith (Miss.) — along with the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) — also participated in the report.

The report accuses three pharmaceutical companies — Danco , GenBioPro and Evita — of failing to adequately keep their drugs from being distributed in ways not compliant with federal regulations. The report also details how the Obama and Biden administrations rolled back the safety guidelines that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) originally attached to approval of the pill in 2000 — and connects those policy changes to a rise in medication abortions.

“Abortion drug companies are putting mothers at risk through their failure to properly oversee the prescription and distribution of their products,” Cassidy said in a statement. “We are seeing that the explosion in online sales of chemical abortion drugs has opened the door to coercion and abuse of women.”

The research, and any attention it brings to the issue, reinvigorates the conservative case for a crackdown on the mail delivery of abortion pills just as crusaders for that cause are coming into the highest levels of power in the administration.

Attorney General Todd Blanche , as he was in the confirmation process, reportedly told anti-abortion advocates that he would work to end the practice of abortion pills being mailed across state lines to skirt state-level abortion restrictions. One step he could take, advocates say, is settling a case Louisiana’s Republican attorney general brought against the FDA last year that seeks to roll back a 2023 rule allowing abortion pills to be permanently available through telehealth and at pharmacies.

A federal appeals court will hear arguments on that case, Louisiana v. FDA, next week.

Marjorie Dannenfelser , president of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America , directly called on Blanche to set a new legal precedent and limit mail delivery and remote prescription of abortion pills.

“Todd Blanche has the opportunity to protect women and save the lives of 15,000 babies every month by settling with the state of Louisiana before Sept. 9,” Dannenfelser said. “He can end this fight with the red states, allow pro-life laws to finally take effect and stop the rise of criminals poisoning mothers with abortion drugs.”

The Senate report also comes as the FDA itself is set to get a new leader: Heidi Overton , a White House health policy aide who has been a staunch critic of the way abortion pills are prescribed and delivered. The FDA is in the process of its own safety study of mifepristone.

Gavin Oxley , spokesperson for Americans United for Life , said the research in the Senate report bolsters the case for the FDA to amp up its restrictions again.

“Abortion drug companies know their drugs are inherently dangerous, leading them to strip away any regulatory mechanism requiring oversight,” Oxley said. “Removing in-person dispensing requirements and reducing adverse event reporting allowed the danger to women to be pushed into the shadows where providers don’t have to face the results of their neglect.”

articles.title: Mangoes recalled in 4 states over salmonella risk
articles.summary: The mangoes were sold from Aug. 10 to 21, some in select Walmart stores.
articles.body:
NEW YORK ( WPI X /NEXSTAR) – If you live in the Northeast and purchased mangoes recently, you may want to check the label.

Panorama Produce, a distributor based in New York, has initiated a recall of mangoes distributed to New York, New Jersey, Connecticut and Pennsylvania over potential salmonella contamination. The recall concerns just over 300 boxes of mangoes sold in the aforementioned states between Aug. 10 and Aug. 21, according to a company announcement posted at the official FDA website.

The recalled mangoes were shipped in boxes labeled with the brand name “Martina.” Individual mangoes have a light blue sticker that reads “Agrofepac, Produce of Mexico.” The label also has a PLU number of 4584 and UPC number 07503061948050.

The company notice indicates the recalled mangoes were sold in “select Walmart stores,” as well.

No illnesses linked to the mangoes had been reported as of Friday, when Panorama Produce announced the recall.

Consumers who believe they may have purchased the mangoes should dispose of the recalled products or return them to the place of purchase. Anyone with questions or concerns can contact Panorama Produce at information@panoramaproduce.com , according to the notice.

Symptoms of salmonella infection often begin to show between six hours and six days after swallowing the bacteria, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Diarrhea, fever, vomiting and stomach cramps are common.

Anyone with suspected salmonella infections are urged to contact a healthcare provider, especially if they are among the most vulnerable groups, or if symptoms worsen to include: bloody diarrhea (or diarrhea that lasts for more than two days); fever of over 102 degrees F; frequent vomiting that prevents the ingestion of liquids; and any sign of dehydration.

More severe illness linked to salmonella can include arterial infections, endocarditis (an infection in the heart), and arthritis. The infection is also blamed for 1.35 million illnesses and 420 deaths in the U.S. annually, according to the FDA.

articles.title: Mozilla launches ad blocking for Firefox on iOS
articles.summary: Mozilla is using Apple’s WebKit Content Blocker technology and the EasyList filter to block ads in Firefox.
articles.body: Mozilla is officially launching ad blocking for Firefox on iOS today, after testing the feature over the past few weeks. The new built-in option will block most third-party ads and trackers before they load on an iPhone, reducing bandwidth use and decluttering mobile websites. Mozilla is using Apple’s WebKit Content Blocker technology and the EasyList filter to block ads in Firefox on iOS, so you won’t need to download and install a separate extension to get it working. The ad blocking is controlled in the settings of Firefox on iOS, and Mozilla is keeping it disabled by default so you have to enable it from settings > browsing > ad blocker. You can also toggle it on or off during a browsing session from the site menu option. Not every ad will be blocked, though. Mozilla says ads served directly by a website or ads shown in search results will still appear. Unsurprisingly, sponsored shortcuts and other sponsored content shown by Firefox when you open a new tab won’t be blocked, either. While this is the first time Firefox has gained ad blocking support on iOS, there are plenty of rival browsers that already offer similar support. Brave, Vivaldi, Opera, and others also have built-in ad blockers on iOS.

articles.title: Fed's Barr: If inflation doesn't moderate, the central bank should raise rates
articles.summary: Federal Reserve governor Michael Barr said Tuesday that if inflation doesn't come down adequately, the central bank should raise interest rates.
articles.body:
Federal Reserve governor Michael Barr said Tuesday that if inflation doesn't come down adequately, the central bank should raise interest rates.

Ahead of the Fed policy meeting in just over two weeks, Barr said the outlook for inflation and the economy will top the agenda.

"If trends in the data give me some confidence that inflation is moderating on a path to 2%, then I think we can take a bit more time to assess our policy stance," Barr said, according to prepared remarks. "However, if inflation appears not to be moderating sufficiently, then I think we should act decisively to raise rates."

The Fed will get two more readings on consumer and wholesale inflation next week before the meeting on Sept. 16. Recent inflation data has been mixed, with back-to-back cooler reports on the Consumer Price Index for June and July and one stickier report on the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the Personal Consumption Expenditures index.

Still, Barr said inflation remains too high, pointing to a series of shocks — from tariffs to the conflict in the Middle East to the rapid AI build-out — that "pushed us off course."

"With inflation above target for a protracted period, there is a risk of broader price pressures taking hold, a risk I am watching closely," he said.

Barr said he views the job market as stable, with relatively low unemployment, and the economy is solid, powered in part by the boom in AI-related business investment.

Last Friday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh put a rate hike back on the table in his closely watched speech in Jackson Hole, Wyo., hinting that current interest rates may not be high enough. "I would be hard-pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive."

Markets are pricing in a 66% chance of a rate hike for the September meeting, up from just above 30% before Warsh's speech.

Jennifer Schonberger is a veteran financial journalist covering markets, the economy, and investing. At Yahoo Finance, she covers the Federal Reserve, Congress, the White House, the Treasury, the SEC, the economy, cryptocurrencies, and the intersection of Washington policy with finance. articles.title: Florida blocks Flock cams on state highways
articles.summary: Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers must be removed from state highways within 30 days.
articles.body: Florida is banning Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers across state highways, as reported earlier by NBC News and local news outlet WUSF. In a memo on Monday, Florida’s Department of Transportation says it’s revoking permits for all license plate readers, adding that they must be removed from state highways within 30 days. As noted in the memo, Florida’s DOT says it’s issuing the order in response to the “recent exponential increase in deployments” of license plate readers, “coupled with concerning reports of misuse, data privacy concerns, and surveillance schemes.” The agency is also halting future requests for license plate reader placements on state roadways. The move comes about a week after Florida Governor Ron DeSantis acknowledged concerns about Flock cameras and license plate readers, saying they’re “out of control. Last month, Texas Governor Greg Abbott froze state spending on Flock cameras as backlash surrounding the cameras grows. Several communities, including Lansing, Michigan; Tempe, Arizona; and Knox County, Tennessee, have ended Flock camera contracts as well.

articles.title: Tim Cook’s legacy isn’t just phones, it’s politics
articles.summary: During his tenure as Apple CEO, Tim Cook deftly navigated geopolitical strain between the US and China.
articles.body: As much as any Apple product released during his time as CEO, Tim Cook’s tenure will be remembered for its ruthlessly efficient tight-rope walk between an autocrat in China and a would-be autocrat in the US. During his 15 years as CEO, Cook steered Apple through relations with both Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump, including escalating conflicts between the two. As Apple’s enmeshment in China raised serious questions about reports of forced labor and censorship, Cook managed to appease Xi while maneuvering around political blowback in the US. And when Trump launched a trade war against China, Cook managed to soften the blow through his White House diplomacy. Cook’s ability to thread the needle between two superpowers helped expand Apple into a multi-trillion-dollar company, while downplaying concerns about civil rights, working conditions, and other serious issues. Cook was the executive who had helped solidify Apple’s manufacturing prowess in China, even before stepping into the role as CEO in 2011. Once at the helm, he had to navigate questions of censorship, data privacy, and forced or child labor reports even before Trump ascended to the presidency. He repeatedly attended meetings with Xi alongside other tech CEOs. The close relationship has put Apple in an awkward position at times. Groups like Human Rights Watch warned that Apple’s actions in China could put it at odds with its stated value of protecting user privacy. In 2014, Apple departed from tech peers like Google by choosing to store some Chinese users’ personal data on servers in mainland China, saying at the time it was meant to improve its services for those users. But the move raised significant concerns that data could be at risk and subject to government censorship, though Apple reportedly stored the encryption keys outside of China. While Apple said an audit of labor conditions at its contractors found no forced labor, it also reportedly lobbied to weaken a US bill that sought to put a stronger onus on American companies to guarantee they weren’t using such a workforce. It’s submitted to Chinese regulations that required it to lower in-app purchase fees but also removed apps from its app store that the government objected to. Beginning in Trump’s first term, Cook also deftly navigated the US president’s whims, and appealed to him with showy displays that cost Apple relatively little. At one memorable tour of a contractor’s Mac Pro manufacturing plant, Cook stood beside Trump as the president falsely claimed that Apple was “building plants in the United States.” (The Texas plant had manufactured Mac Pros for years, and while Apple was building something in Austin at the time, it was a new campus, not a manufacturing facility.) Cook knew how to pick his battles, balancing his relationship with Trump with maintaining confidence from staff and customers. After Trump imposed immigration restrictions on seven Muslim-majority countries in 2017, for instance, Cook told employees it was “not a policy we support.” Trump kicked off the initial trade war with China in his first term, leading China to impose its own tariffs on US goods in response. Eventually, Cook was able to win Apple a reprieve from some of the high tariffs imposed by the US on goods from China, such as the Apple Watch. In Trump’s second term, Cook’s support became more visible and his pushback more muted. Cook attended Trump’s second inauguration alongside many other tech CEOs, and donated $1 million to his inauguration committee. After Cook and other CEOs attended a film screening of Amazon’s documentary on Melania Trump hours after federal agents shot and killed protester Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, Cook assured employees he was “heartbroken” by the situation and “had a good conversation with the president this week where I shared my views.” But similar to the stunt at the Texas manufacturing plant, Cook continued to present Trump with useful trophies to tout his policies — in August 2025, that came in the form of a gold and glass statue, awarded to the president as a symbol of Apple’s “Made in the USA” efforts. And to stave off more costly tariffs, he cut deals to bring more manufacturing to the US. Walking that line let Cook and Apple do what they do best: pumping out a new version of the iPhone year after year, with the supply chain and trade conditions in place to make it happen. It’s only now that the AI-fueled RAM shortage is forcing Apple’s hand to raise prices, according to Cook. But even as Cook’s time as CEO has come to an end, it seems he won’t soon shake his role as Apple’s geopolitical negotiator-in-chief. In announcing Cook’s ascension to executive chairman, Apple wrote, Cook would continue “engaging with policymakers around the world.”

articles.title: Florida and Texas move to block Flock cameras over privacy concerns | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Flock's searchable network of 130,000 license plate cameras around the U.S. have sparked bipartisan privacy and civil liberties concerns.
articles.body:
The states of Florida and Texas are moving to end their relationship with surveillance giant Flock, as the company faces increasing backlash over privacy concerns and misuse of its tracking technology.

Florida’s Department of Transportation sa i d in a memo on Monday that it will cease using license plate readers across the state’s highways, such as Flock’s cameras, citing “concerning reports of misuse, data privacy concerns, and surveillance schemes.” The state now has 30 days to remove the cameras.

The decision comes days after Florida governor Ron DeSantis called the license plate reading technology “out of control” in remarks during a press conference last Wednesday.

Florida follows similar action by Texas, which last week ordered state agencies to stop funding Flock cameras. Texas governor Greg Abbott’s office cited abuse of the surveillance system, including the recent indictment of a Lufkin, Texas police officer with 100 felony counts related to allegedly searching Flock’s database to track people without authorization.

Abbott’s office did not say which agencies would be affected, but local media reports that Dallas could be broadly affected, as officials say there are hundreds of Flock cameras operating throughout the city.

The move comes amid rising bipartisan concerns over privacy and civil liberties concerns, following reports of cybersecurity issues , police abusing their access to Flock’s database to stalk their ex-partners, and accuracy issues that have led to police stops and wrongful arrests . Recent reporting shows that Flock cameras are moving away from scanning license plates and are also working to identify and track people .

Flock currently has around 130,000 license plate readers across the United States. The company has faced pushback from communities whose residents say they do not want Flock in their neighborhoods. Several towns, including Evanston, Illinois , Cambridge, Massachusetts , and Eugene, Oregon , reported that Flock reinstalled or reactivated their cameras, despite local officials terminating their contracts with the company.

TechCrunch contacted Flock to ask if the company plans to allow Florida and Texas to remove their cameras, or if Flock plans to reinstall or reactivate them. A Flock spokesperson did not respond to our request for comment.

Canada responded three days later with retaliatory tariffs on roughly $20 billion of annual U.S. imports, matching Trump's latest tariffs dollar for dollar. Those counter-tariffs are scheduled to take effect Sept. 8, ⁠⁠according to Reuters (3).

articles.title: AIR raises $50M to help companies vet the skills and add-ons AI agents use | TechCrunch
articles.summary: AIR's platform can discover agents running at a company, continuously vets any skills and add-ons they use, and blocks any unwanted behaviour.
articles.body:
As companies start giving AI agents access to an increasing portion of their systems, a nascent software supply chain seems to be forming around the new tooling AI agents are using: skills, plugins, MCP servers, and add-ons that let them interact with the internet.

AI security startup AIR believes companies will need a way to monitor that supply chain, and it’s now coming out of stealth with $50 million raised across two seed rounds to build that product.

Founded by Yair Saban (CEO) and Niv Hoffman (CTO), veterans of Israel’s Unit 8200 intelligence corps, where they worked on offensive cybersecurity, AIR offers a platform that can discover agents running inside companies, continuously vet any skills, tools, and components those agents use, and block them from interacting with software or external sources that don’t pass security criteria. It also offers a marketplace of vetted add-ons and skills for AI agents.

The funding rounds closed within weeks of each other, Saban told TechCrunch, with the first round raising $10 million, and the second $40 million. Sequoia led the first round, while Greenoaks led the second, Saban said. Swish, Netz, and Zach Frankel (president of Cognition), Yinon Costica (co-founder of Wiz), Ofir Erlich (co-founder of Eon), Anne Neuberger, Omer Adam, Varun Anand (co-founder of Clay), and other angel investors also participated.

AIR’s pitch goes thusly: The way AI agents are used wholesale at companies is beginning to resemble operating systems, but the tools they use, or the software they can install, aren’t yet being given the kind of oversight we give to drivers or applications.

“In the early 2000s, whenever you installed a driver, the driver didn’t need to be signed. Today, every time you install a driver, you see a signature saying who signed it, because the driver is actually loading code into the kernel,” Saban said. “You don’t have that with skills or plugins or MCPs, and it’s a shame, because it’s the same mechanism, it’s the same lesson, but we haven’t learned it.”

The big risk, he argues, is that as AI agents start working more autonomously across databases, enterprise systems, and connecting to the internet, attackers can poison the content an AI agent consumes instead of attacking it directly.

The startup says it can solve that with a visibility product that finds agents active across a company’s environment, as well as identifies employees who use AI tools unapproved by IT departments or those who use personal accounts. Then, it uses an enforcement layer that hooks into agents to intercept and analyze actions, like loading a skill or fetching content from the internet. Lastly, AIR also checks the tools, add-ons, or software an agent wants to use against a whitelist the startup maintains.

Saban says the startup maintains this whitelist by evaluating skills and add-ons openly available on the internet for changes and malicious behavior, as a previously approved skill could become risky if a package it downloads changes, or its developer’s account is compromised. He added that AIR’s platform currently filters out about 27% of the add-ons and skills it finds online.

AIR claims it has more than 20 customers, and Saban said roughly a quarter of these are large enterprises. He said the company has so far seen the strongest demand in heavily regulated industries, particularly financial services and pharmaceutical companies.

However, AIR is hardly alone in this space. Noma Security offers discovery, access controls and runtime monitoring for agents, MCP servers and skills, while Zenity sells security and governance tools that work similarly. Astrix Security ‘s identity platform also lets companies discover and control agents and MCP servers, and Operant AI offers agent protections as well as an MCP gateway.

There is significant venture money chasing the category, too. Zenity raised a $125 million Series C in August, while Noma raised a $100 million Series B last year.

Saban thinks AIR’s moat lies in its ability to continuously vet the skills and add-ons ecosystem growing around AI agents. “Continuously vetting skills and plugin websites, this is a hard mission to do. Gaining visibility over the endpoint, that is easy. Everybody’s going to do it. It’s hard to create a moat around that,” he said.

And while the CEO acknowledged that AI labs and providers will eventually build in security checks and policies to filter out malicious skill and tool usage, he thinks companies will still want to buy an independent product that works across vendors.

“This is not a scanning problem, it is a continuous re-verification problem,” Bogomil Balkansky, partner at Sequoia, told TechCrunch in an emailed statement. “Inspecting every skill, plugin, MCP server and sub-agent an enterprise’s agents touch, re-inspecting each one every time it changes, in real time and across an entire company’s agent fleet, is an infrastructure problem long before it is a security problem. Air has spent the last year building that pipeline. You do not catch up to it by writing a better scanner.”

AIR currently has around 40 employees. Saban said the new capital will primarily go toward hiring researchers and expanding the company’s go-to-market efforts in the U.S. and Europe.

articles.title: Carney Says Trade Talks Can Resume If US Stops ‘Throwing Shade’
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said he still believes there’s a “mutually beneficial” trade deal to be done with the US, but discussions can’t resume while Trump...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Prime Minister Mark Carney said he still believes there's a "mutually beneficial" trade deal to be done with the US, but discussions can't resume while Trump administration officials are publicly insulting Canada.

Carney, speaking Tuesday morning to reporters in Ottawa, was asked about President Donald Trump's move to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America, along with other comments from US officials denigrating Canada's military and economy.

"There's a positive opportunity that has always existed with the United States for a mutually beneficial trade deal that respects Canadian sovereignty," the prime minister said. "When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions."

Asked specifically about remarks from members of Trump's cabinet insulting Canada's armed forces, Carney called those comments "beneath their office."

On Monday night, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made a post mocking two women in a Canadian youth cadet program.

Earlier Monday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent scoffed at the idea the US was in a trade war with its northern neighbor, asking if Canada was going to "take their two submarines from the Edmonton mall and sic them on us." That's a reference to a visitor attraction that was removed from the West Edmonton Mall in 2005.

Trade talks between the US and Canada broke down on Aug. 21, and Trump imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports the next day. Canada has announced retaliatory duties set to take effect Sept. 8 on a roughly equal amount of US goods.

Speaking Tuesday, Carney said the talks collapsed due to an "accumulation of issues," including on proposed tariff arrangements affecting key industries such as auto manufacturing.

US officials have taken the view that those sectors "would be subsidiaries, effectively, of the United States' industries, or would put in place terms where those industries would be gradually wound down in Canada," Carney said. "We're not going to accept those terms."

Carney added that Trump's attempt to crush Canada's auto industry is also "misguided."

"The United States auto industry is made stronger by the Canadian and the Mexican auto industries. And at a time of big, big change in autos, it's important that we work together," he said.

articles.title: Explainer-What's behind the selloff in world bond markets?
articles.summary: By Dhara Ranasinghe and Harry Robertson LONDON, Sept 1 (Reuters) - Government borrowing costs from the United States to Germany and Japan are at or near mult...
articles.body:
LONDON, Sept 1 (Reuters) - Government borrowing costs from the United States to Germany and Japan are at or near multi-decade peaks on heightened worries about inflation and rising interest rates, along with nagging anxiety about their debt loads.

Elevated bond yields could squeeze households ‌and companies as well as exacerbating government finances.

Here's a look at what's behind the move in some major economies.

Japan's 10-year bond yield hit 3% ‌on Tuesday for the first time since 1996, a milestone for an economy still emerging from an era of ultra-low rates.

Britain's 30-year borrowing costs are at 30-year highs, and German and French 10-year yields are ​at levels last seen in 2011 and 2008 respectively.

U.S. 30-year yields rose to their highest since 2007 earlier in August.

A renewed rise in oil prices on U.S.-Iran tensions is driving yields higher as elevated inflation leaves traders braced for more rate hikes.

It adds to concerns about rising borrowing. The U.S. debt pile just crossed $40 trillion, while debt as a share of economic output is at or above 100% across the G7 group of major economies, bar Germany.

A hawkish speech by U.S. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh at the Jackson Hole symposium has ‌also added to traders' rate hike bets.

Bond ⁠yields set the tone for borrowing costs across economies, from government debt to mortgages to student and car loans. Rising rates make borrowing and spending less attractive and can slow economic growth.

For instance, U.S. 30-year mortgage rates have risen to a one-year high of nearly 6.7% ⁠as yields have climbed on 10-year U.S. Treasuries.

Rising yields mean governments face higher costs as they roll over debt. After a borrowing surge and rise in yields, Britain's interest bill of almost 4% of output is now roughly double its pre-pandemic decade average, its fiscal watchdog said in March, and eclipses the defence budget.

Bond yields also ripple through markets. Higher yields theoretically make stocks ​less ​attractive, though strong earnings have kept equities buoyant. And heavily leveraged hedge funds, which trade across ​countless markets, could come under pressure, too.

WHERE DO TECH HYPERSCALERS COME ‌INTO THIS?

A surge in bond sales to fund AI investments is another factor pushing up bond yields.

Analysts point to the laws of supply and demand: if there is a jump in need for borrowing, lenders can charge higher interest rates, pushing up yields.
authors: By Dhara Ranasinghe and Harry Robertson

articles.title: What a smart firewall does and why it matters on home Wi-Fi
articles.summary: Router firewalls and software firewalls serve different roles in protecting your home Wi-Fi from unwanted traffic and suspicious connections.
articles.body: Most of us think of home Wi-Fi as the invisible connection that lets a laptop stream a movie, a phone display photos and a printer work from across the room. In practice, it is also the meeting point for many devices, accounts and types of information. A typical home network may include computers, phones, tablets, smart speakers, televisions, cameras, printers and connected appliances. These devices regularly send and receive data. Some of that traffic is expected, such as opening a bank website or downloading a software update. Other traffic may be unwanted or suspicious. That is where a firewall comes in. A firewall is a security system that checks network connections and applies rules about which traffic should be allowed. Think of it as a doorman for digital connections. It does not know everything about every visitor, but it can help prevent some unexpected traffic from reaching a device. Understanding how firewalls work, where they fit and what they can and cannot protect against can help you make smarter choices about securing your home Wi-Fi. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com FBI SAYS RUSSIAN HACKERS HIJACKED OLD WI-FI ROUTERS Router firewall vs software firewall Your router is the box that connects your home to the internet and sends Wi-Fi throughout the house. Many home routers include a built-in firewall. Because it sits at the gateway, this router firewall can help protect devices connected to your home network from certain unwanted connections coming from the internet. A router firewall is useful because one device can provide a basic layer of protection for the network as a whole. It can help reduce direct exposure for computers, phones and other connected equipment. However, its settings and capabilities depend on the router model, its software and how it was configured. A software firewall runs on an individual device, such as a Windows PC or Mac. It can add another layer of awareness and control at the device level. This becomes especially useful when a laptop leaves home, connects to a different network or needs to distinguish between applications running on that computer. TRAVEL MISTAKE PUTS PHONE, LAPTOP AND STREAMING ACCOUNTS AT RISK The two types can work together. A router firewall and a software firewall serve different purposes. The router helps guard the network's front door, while the software firewall helps watch activity involving a particular device. What inbound and outbound traffic mean The terms sound technical, but the basic idea is straightforward. Inbound traffic is data traveling toward your device. For example, a website may send information back to your browser after you request a page, or a remote computer may try to connect to a service on your network. Some inbound traffic is expected, especially when it responds to a connection you started. Other inbound traffic may be unexpected. Outbound traffic is data leaving your device. Opening a webpage, sending an email, uploading a photograph or syncing a file all involve outbound activity. If an unfamiliar program tries to connect to the internet, that may also be outbound traffic. CHEAP STREAMING BOX COULD HIJACK YOUR HOME INTERNET A firewall may use rules, application information and other signals to decide whether a connection looks familiar or requires attention. Depending on the operating system and security product, it may alert you, allow the connection or block it. The goal is to help ordinary online activity continue while making unusual network behavior more visible and manageable. Why network awareness deserves more attention now Online banking and shopping place sensitive information at the center of ordinary internet use. You may sign in to a bank, enter a card number, review a medical bill or manage a retirement account from the same computer you use for entertainment. BEWARE OF HACKERS SHOWING UP PRETENDING TO BE IT Remote work adds another reason to pay attention. A home laptop may handle work documents, personal files and video meetings throughout the day. If an unfamiliar application begins communicating online, security tools that provide additional context can help you understand what the computer is doing. A firewall cannot tell whether every website, email or message is honest. A scammer may persuade someone to visit a legitimate-looking page or approve an action that appears convincing. A firewall provides one layer of protection, while your decisions remain an important part of staying safe. YOUR BANK MAY STOP TEXTING YOU SIX-DIGIT CODES What a firewall can and cannot do A firewall can help control certain network connections. It may reduce exposure to some unsolicited inbound traffic and help identify unusual activity involving applications. It can also add a layer of protection when a device connects to networks outside the home. A firewall cannot make a weak password strong or determine whether someone is being tricked by a convincing text message. It also cannot replace antivirus protection, software updates, multifactor authentication, secure router settings or reliable backups. No firewall can guarantee that files, accounts or devices will never be compromised. Some threats arrive through activity you intentionally start, such as opening a malicious attachment or entering information into a fake website. Other threats may exploit weaknesses in outdated software. Those situations call for additional defenses and safer habits. HOTEL WI-FI PHISHING ATTACK TARGETS MICROSOFT LOGINS Home Wi-Fi basics worth checking A few simple router and Wi-Fi settings can strengthen your home network and reduce unnecessary security risks. Secure your router settings Start with the router. Use the security mode recommended by the manufacturer or internet provider and avoid leaving the administrator password at its default. The administrator password controls important router settings and should be different from the Wi-Fi password. Keep your router updated Install router firmware updates when they are offered. Firmware is the built-in software that helps the router operate. Updates may improve performance, fix problems or address security weaknesses. Strengthen your Wi-Fi access Use a strong, unique Wi-Fi password. If your router offers a guest network, consider using it for visitors or devices that do not need access to your main network. Check connected devices Review the list of connected devices occasionally so you know what is using your Wi-Fi. If you see a device you do not recognize, investigate it and change your Wi-Fi password if needed. Replace outdated routers Consider replacing a router that no longer receives security updates or cannot support current security standards. Check the manufacturer's documentation rather than assuming that a newer Wi-Fi label automatically gives you stronger security. A firewall provides one layer of protection A firewall works best as part of a broader security setup that protects your devices, accounts and important files. Keep software and devices updated Keep your operating system, browser, apps and router updated. Turn on automatic updates when that option is available. Protect important accounts with multifactor authentication Use multifactor authentication for banking, email and other important accounts. Multifactor authentication adds a second verification step, such as an approval on your phone, after your password. Watch for suspicious links and requests Be cautious with unexpected links, attachments and urgent requests for payment or personal information. Scammers often rely on urgency to get you to act before you have time to question what is happening. Be careful with remote-access requests Before approving a remote-access request, confirm who is asking and why. If an alert appears, read it carefully rather than automatically allowing or dismissing it. Strengthen your firewall with antivirus protection and backups Firewalls, antivirus software and backups each protect you in a different way. A firewall helps control network connections, antivirus software detects and responds to malicious software, and reliable backups can help you recover important files if they are damaged, deleted or locked by ransomware. Together, these protections create a stronger defense than any one tool can provide alone. When choosing antivirus protection, look for real-time malware and ransomware detection, phishing protection, automatic security updates and coverage for all the devices you use. Some products also include device-level firewall protection or cloud backup, but features, storage limits and compatibility can vary by platform. Visit CyberGuy’s best antivirus protection guide for our current recommendations, comparisons and special offers for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. Protecting the files you cannot replace Your computer may hold years of family photos, tax returns, medical records, scanned IDs, insurance documents and other files that would be difficult or impossible to replace. That makes protecting your data just as important as protecting the computer itself. Understand the ransomware risk Ransomware is malicious software that can lock or encrypt your files and then demand payment to restore access. A firewall may help block or limit some suspicious connections, but ransomware can reach a device in other ways. Strong security habits and reliable backups give you a better chance of recovering if something goes wrong. Follow the 3-2-1 backup approach A useful guideline is the 3-2-1 backup strategy: keep three copies of important data on two different types of storage, with at least one copy stored separately from your computer. CISA guidance recommends this approach as one way to improve your ability to recover from ransomware. Make sure your backups can actually help Backups work best when they are automatic, current and separated from the same incident affecting your computer. Test a few backed-up files occasionally to make sure you can open them. When practical, keep at least one backup disconnected from your computer or otherwise isolated from routine activity. CISA recommends offline backups because some ransomware can also reach connected storage. Protect cloud backup accounts with strong, unique passwords and multifactor authentication. Norton AntiVirus Plus includes 2 GB of PC Cloud Backup on eligible Windows systems. Know what to do if ransomware strikes If your files suddenly become encrypted, disconnect the affected computer from the network if you can do so safely. CISA recommends isolating affected systems, including disconnecting them from Wi-Fi when necessary, to help prevent the infection from spreading. Avoid rushing to pay a ransom or deleting potential evidence. Preserve messages and notes about what happened and check whether clean backups are available. Consider contacting a qualified cybersecurity professional for help. If you believe an account may also have been exposed, change important passwords from a separate, trusted device. FCC ROUTER RULE RAISES QUESTIONS ABOUT FUTURE UPDATES Kurt's key takeaways A firewall does a lot of work you may never see, and that is exactly why it can be easy to overlook. Your router firewall helps protect the network at home, while a software firewall can watch connections involving a specific computer wherever you take it. I would use both when available, but I would never count on a firewall by itself. Strong passwords, multifactor authentication, current software, antivirus protection and dependable backups all cover risks that a firewall cannot handle. The bigger point is visibility. Most of us have dozens of connections happening behind the scenes every time we use a computer. A good firewall gives you another set of eyes on that activity and another opportunity to stop something suspicious before it goes further. When was the last time you checked whether your router firewall was enabled and which devices are connected to your home Wi-Fi? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: CDC, Pennsylvania clash over measles deaths
articles.summary: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is disputing two measles deaths reported by Pennsylvania and excluding them from its official weekly tally of deaths, a radical departure from the agency’s normal practice of accepting and including a state’s data. The decision to question Pennsylvania’s classification of measles deaths represents a key test for…
articles.body:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is disputing two measles deaths reported by Pennsylvania and excluding them from its official weekly tally of deaths, a radical departure from the agency’s normal practice of accepting and including a state’s data.

The decision to question Pennsylvania’s classification of measles deaths represents a key test for new CDC Director Erica Schwartz, who took charge of the agency last month amid a pledge to operate independently from Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

It also inserts the nation’s public health agency into the middle of a political feud between Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) and Kennedy about whether the deaths were a result of measles, or whether measles was present but unrelated.

The deaths were not included on the CDC’s website, which is typically updated on Fridays. The update was delayed until Sunday, when the agency’s website was edited multiple times.

“This week’s measles outbreaks update will not include the two measles-associated deaths reported by the Pennsylvania Department of Health on August 25 while CDC reviews additional information regarding the circumstances and causes of death,” an asterisk on the agency website states . “At this time, available information does not establish whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths or whether the individuals died from other causes while infected with measles. CDC will update the national count as additional information becomes available.”

Details on the two deaths released by the Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) were vague, leaving a void of information. The state first disclosed the deaths last Tuesday, and Shapiro held a press conference to discuss them shortly afterwards.

One of the two deaths involved a newborn with a ruptured spleen. Details of the second case have not been disclosed. The only other details shared were that the patients were unvaccinated and from Lancaster County, and both tested positive for the measles virus.

Neil Ruhland, a spokesman for the Pennsylvania DOH, said every reported measles case is “thoroughly reviewed to confirm it meets the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC) case definition for a measles case.”

Ruhland said the agency has “provided all required epidemiological data to the CDC regarding the two measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania. DOH values its long-standing collaborative relationship with professional staff at the CDC and will continue to work with federal partners moving forward to address the ongoing measles outbreak.”

Shapiro and state health officials said the deaths were “measles-associated,” a term the state uses when measles is present, but the disease may not be identified the immediate cause of death.

“CDC is committed to providing the public with accurate information. The two measles-associated deaths announced by Pennsylvania have not been confirmed based on the information currently available to CDC,” Grace Davis Jamison, a spokeswoman for the federal Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), told The Hill in a statement. “CDC therefore delayed its weekly update while seeking additional information to ensure its national reporting is accurate.”

Jamison did not say which CDC officials made the decision to question Pennsylvania’s reporting and delay updating the data.

Pennsylvania is in the midst of a growing measles outbreak that has sickened 497 people and hospitalized 87 as of Monday. During his press conference last week, Shapiro put the blame on Kennedy and the Trump administration for sowing doubt about vaccines.

“When the information we see coming from the federal government, in some cases, isn’t driven by facts and by science, it makes it even more confusing for parents, and that has a serious impact,” Shapiro said .

Kennedy denied any responsibility for the drop in vaccination rates. In a social media post, he suggested the deaths might have been “fabricated by one of the Governor’s hopeful staffers” to score political points.

“Governor Shapiro’s unseemly rush to Lancaster County to convene a national press conference and his giddy delight in announcing two measles deaths was a morose commentary on the contemporary political dialogue,” Kennedy wrote on the social platform X.

The CDC’s official X account then doubled down on Kennedy’s skepticism.

“We appreciate Secretary Kennedy’s efforts to clarify conflicting information from Pennsylvania officials about whether the two reported deaths were caused by measles. CDC is working to determine what actually occurred,” the agency said Thursday. “Under President Trump’s and Secretary Kennedy’s leadership, CDC will follow the facts and tell the American people the truth.”

The CDC’s delay and refusal to accept Pennsylvania’s data is not typically how the agency operates regarding measles. CDC relies on state health officials to investigate and report measles cases to the federal government.

Measles is considered an urgent “notifiable condition,” and standard protocol is to notify the CDC by phone within 24 hours of a confirmed case.

“CDC doesn’t adjudicate those cases or deaths,” said Deb Houry, the former chief medical officer at the CDC during last year’s West Texas measles outbreak that resulted in the deaths of two unvaccinated school-aged children.

In Texas, Houry said the CDC was notified of the deaths by the state health department and then they were included in the agency’s measles dashboard.

When New Mexico reported an unvaccinated adult died and measles was found in his system, Houry said CDC recorded that death as well, even though it was under investigation.

If the CDC starts to question what states report, it could undermine the trust and needed collaboration between the federal government and states, experts said.

Houry said she was disappointed by the political tone of CDC’s messaging.

“When there’s a time of 400 plus measles cases and growing in the community, the focus should be on what can be done in the community versus this back and forth. So it’s very disappointing that this is what we’re seeing,” Houry said. “I had high hopes for Dr. Schwartz, but the fact that she is not working collaboratively with the state on this is not a good sign, and the focus really needs to be on what is being done in these communities.”

articles.title: US strikes IRGC targets in Iran in response to attacks on American forces
articles.summary: The U.S. military struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets inside Iran on Tuesday following Tehran’s attacks on U.S. military assets in the region, the U.S. Central Command (Centcom) announced. articles.body:
The U.S. military struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets inside Iran on Tuesday following Tehran’s attacks on U.S. military assets in the region, the U.S. Central Command (Centcom) announced.

The fresh round of strikes, which began at noon, came after the IRGC fired one-way attack drones and missiles at the King Hussein and Azraq military bases in Jordan on Monday.

The IRGC also targeted Centcom forces and helicopters at Al Minhad Air Base in the United Arab Emirates, according to Iranian media.

“The strikes follow recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region,” Centcom posted on social media .

The renewed military operations in recent days follow a tense, unofficial monthlong pause in strikes.

President Trump, in a Truth Social post Tuesday afternoon, warned Iran against further escalation and said the U.S. strikes are “retaliation” for Iran’s “failed attempt” to deploy sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz and for the attacks against U.S. bases in Jordan.

“If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level,” Trump said.

He further warned that the U.S. was holding back a larger military attack, that is “waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran!”

As the war passes its six-month mark, Trump is confronting Iran’s resistance to capitulation in the face of U.S. military power and little to no progress in talks to get Tehran to give up its nuclear program and release its hold on the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s effective chokehold on the strait has blocked global oil and gas exports, and contributed to higher energy prices across the world.

The U.S. has imposed a naval blockade against Iranian oil exports in the strait and has tried to secretly ferry stranded tankers through the waterway and clear Iranian mines along the shipping routes.

The U.S. military had redirected 84 commercial ships, disabled three and boarded another two since resuming the blockade in July, Centcom announced in an update on Tuesday.

In rare conciliatory remarks, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Tuesday said Iran was prepared to return to a memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in June with the U.S. if Trump returns to commitments in the document. Pezeshkian was speaking at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Kyrgyzstan, The Associated Press reported, citing Iranian state media.

The MOU fell apart as Iran pointed to text in the document that it believed gave them control over the Strait of Hormuz and that the U.S. contested.

Pezeshkian’s statements came as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned of increasing economic pressure against Iran under the so-called Operation Economic Outcast.

Bessent issued a global threat to “economically asphyxiate” the Iranian regime, saying Tehran would only return to the MOU and talks with the U.S. under severe financial pressure.

“We are tracking down the IRGC’s assets … We know where in the British Virgin Islands your accounts are, at these trust companies, we know the $100 million houses you have around the world, we’re going to freeze those.”

articles.title: Congress Sends Funding Bill to Avert US Shutdown to Trump
articles.summary: Congress cleared funding legislation to avert an Oct. 1 government shutdown, sidestepping, at least temporarily, the partisan warfare that led to repeated di...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Congress cleared funding legislation to avert an Oct. 1 government shutdown, sidestepping, at least temporarily, the partisan warfare that led to repeated disruptions over the last year.

By a vote of 370 to 48, the House Tuesday overwhelmingly passed the stopgap funding bill to finance the government through Dec. 11, pushing funding battles until after the November midterm elections. The measure, which the Senate approved in early August, now heads to President Donald Trump.

Trump has vowed not to sign any legislation until Congress passes new voter identification requirements. But he could simply allow the bill to become law after 10 days, a passive stance he took with bipartisan housing legislation earlier in the summer.

A stopgap bill is needed because none of the 12 annual spending bills for the new fiscal year have been approved by Congress. Enactment of the legislation puts off until after the election hard decisions about potential increases to the Pentagon budget and Republican proposals to further cut social safety net programs.

"This bill contains no poison pills and no partisan riders," House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole said just before the vote, adding that the legislation has the White House's support.

Passage of the stopgap comes as congressional Republicans are prepared to punt consideration of a separate $95 billion bill intended to provide emergency Iran war funding until after the elections. A proposal to increase the base Pentagon budget by $350 billion paid for in part by anti-fraud efforts in healthcare programs is also being kicked into the autumn.

The smooth sailing for the stopgap contrasts to the vitriolic battles over funding that characterized most of this fiscal year. A battle over expiring Obamacare premium subsidies led Senate Democrats last year to trigger the longest government shutdown in history while a separate battle over immigration enforcement funding led to a record shuttering of the Department of Homeland Security earlier this year.

Another shutdown before the midterms would have resulted in lengthy waits at airport screenings and other disruptions, risking turning off voters in both parties.

articles.title: Tim Cook hands over reins of Apple, but remains Trump whisperer
articles.summary: Apple’s Tim Cook handed over the reins as CEO to John Ternus on Tuesday, but the technology giant won’t be losing his political clout and connections to Washington. In his new role as executive chair of Apple’s board, Cook will focus on policy, leveraging the political muscle he’s built over the past 15 years to…
articles.body:
Apple’s Tim Cook handed over the reins as CEO to John Ternus on Tuesday, but the technology giant won’t be losing his political clout and connections to Washington.

In his new role as executive chair of Apple’s board, Cook will focus on policy, leveraging the political muscle he’s built over the past 15 years to navigate the White House’s shifting trade policy and fierce competition with China.

Cook is a “major asset to Apple” regardless of his position, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, told The Hill on Monday.

“It’s not just for Apple, but [Cook] plays a key role for the tech industry going into this landscape with AI, political debates in the U.S. around data centers, the U.S.-China battle for tech supremacy,” Ives said.

Announcing his decision to step down as CEO in April, Apple said Cook will “assist with certain aspects of the company” as executive chair, including “engaging with policymakers around the world.” Specifically, Cook told Ternus he will manage Apple’s relationships with President Trump and the Chinese government, Bloomberg reported .

Cook, who served as Apple’s CEO since 2011, is among a handful of technology leaders who built a friendly rapport with Trump, despite occasional tensions in the president’s first and second terms.

Shortly after Cook announced he would step down as CEO, Trump said he has “ always been a big fan ” of the executive, calling him “an amazing manager and leader.”

Technology analysts predict Cook’s relationship with Trump will be key to ensuring Apple’s success as Ternus — a product designer with little political experience — steps into the role.

“Ternus really is a product guy … it makes sense for Cook to say, ‘Look, John, you run the product show right now, and I’ll handle these policy and relationship issues while you get your feet on the ground,’” said David Pogue, a veteran technology journalist and CBS News “Sunday Morning” correspondent who recently published the book “Apple: The First 50 Years.”

While Cook previously served as Apple’s chief operating officer, tackling sales, operations and supply chain logistics, Ternus’s 25 years at Apple were spent on hardware and product design.

The new CEO played a major role in the release of new products like the iPad and AirPods, most recently serving as the company’s senior vice president of hardware engineering.

Ternus is walking into the role under pressure to tackle the company’s lagging development of artificial intelligence and the rollout of Apple’s newest products at the company’s annual event next week.

Unlike many CEO transitions, Ternus will be able to focus on this with assistance from Cook and his 15 years of working with governments around the world.

The former CEO’s political maneuvering has been on full display during Trump’s first and second terms, including during the height of Trump’s tariff war last year, when Trump announced massive “reciprocal” tariffs on other nations, including China.

The tariffs exposed Apple to potential losses since the majority of its products are made in China and other parts of Asia.

But two days after Trump’s announcement in April 2025, Trump exempted electronics like phones, computers, routers and semiconductor chips, saying he “helped” Cook and “that whole business” by doing so. Apple regained its $3 trillion market cap following the exemption.

Reports later circulated that Cook spoke with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick about the potential impact of the tariffs on iPhone prices, but he did not publicly criticize the president or his trade decisions.

The move drew scrutiny from Democrats, who pointed to Cook’s $1 million donation to Trump’s inauguration fund and attendance at the ceremony. Other technology CEOs — like Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Amazon’s Jeff Bezos — also donated large sums to the fund and stood behind the president during his swearing-in.

“If the tariffs went into effect, it would have been disastrous for Apple and its shareholders and its customers. It would have perhaps doubled the price of an iPhone. It doesn’t take a detective to realize that if Cook could get Trump’s ear on this tariff decision, then it would benefit Apple and its constituents,” Pogue said.

In the following month, Trump announced a deal to lower tariffs on Chinese imports to 30 percent from 145 percent, adding he spoke to Cook that morning, during which the then-CEO vowed to open more plants in the U.S.

But at the same time, Cook faced public pressure from Trump to reshore Apple manufacturing from India to the U.S.

About two months later, Cook joined Trump in the Oval Office to announce an additional $100 billion investment into U.S. manufacturing, bringing the company’s total investment to $600 billion. During the event, Cook gifted Trump a glass dish with a 24-karat gold base designed by a former Marine who works at Apple.

“This is all either sickeningly subservient or shrewdly strategic, depending on your politics,” Pogue added.

While donating funds or gifts to governments is nothing new for business, Trump’s emphasis on personal relationships with leaders, combined with his fluctuating temperament, makes getting along with the president more important than ever now, experts said.

“We have a president who takes perceived slights much more seriously than various others, and so the business people of the world, whose primary job is to do well in business, of course, see that as an opportunity and a necessity to please the president,” Pogue said.

Damaged relationships between companies and the Trump administration have proved costly before. Ives pointed to this year’s spat between the Pentagon and AI firm Anthropic, which lost a contract after CEO Dario Amodei demanded certain safety guardrails for the use of AI on the battlefield.

The disagreement quickly became a culture turf war between Anthropic and the Trump administration, and it showcased how businesses could suffer as a result of disagreement with the government.

“I don’t think other tech companies want to be in that role,” Ives said.

Cook’s expertise on global affairs — especially China — is also likely to benefit Apple’s interests, as the former CEO balanced the line between maintaining relations with the Chinese government and appeasing Trump’s demands for domestic manufacturing.

“Trump’s always viewed Cook, despite some of the speed bumps, as someone that’s very plugged into not just the tech world, but also when it comes to China, and his importance is going to remain,” Ives said.

Over the next few weeks, all eyes are on Ternus and the direction Apple takes on AI as a product builder himself.

Cook, in a Monday memo to staff, wrote that “few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does.”

“It’s pretty clear that Apple has lagged when it comes to AI, so I think they are smart to put a product person as CEO because I think they really need to push more aggressively into AI hardware, AI-era hardware,” Sarah Kreps, director of the Tech Policy Institute in the Cornell Brooks School of Public Policy, told The Hill.
