articles.body:
President Trump on Tuesday announced the selection of Darrell Scott, a pastor and longtime Trump supporter, to be the tobacco health adviser for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Trump announced Scott’s new role in a Truth Social post , citing his longtime advocacy for “America’s Underserved Communities.”

“For far too long, tobacco-related disease has taken an enormous toll on American Families, including Communities that have too often been overlooked and underserved. Pastor Scott understands these Communities, and the challenges they face, and he knows how to bring people together to get RESULTS,” Trump wrote.

“Delivering on a Campaign promise, his work will help ensure that we take a serious look at how we can better protect Americans from dangerous tobacco products, while supporting solutions to reduce harm and SAVE LIVES,” the president added.

What health policy expertise Scott brings to the role remains unclear. The Hill has reached out to the Department of Health and Human Services for comment.

Scott shared Trump’s announcement on his own social media but did not give any additional comment.

He has been a supporter of Trump’s presidency since 2016, including cofounding the National Diversity Coalition for Trump.

The position within the CDC will be Scott’s first official role within Trump’s administration, though he has previously identified himself as the president’s “senior advisor.”

The Trump administration has rolled back longstanding efforts to reduce tobacco use, including ending the CDC’s Tips From Former Smokers ad campaign launched in 2012 and its Office on Smoking and Health, which has effectively become one of many “zombie programs.”

The Food and Drug Administration has also granted marketing authorization to several flavored tobacco pouches on the basis that they are less harmful than cigarettes. RAI Services Co. — a subsidiary of Reynolds American, which owns brands like Newport, Camel and Pall Mall — was the biggest corporate donor to Trump’s 2024 campaign.

articles.title: Abortion rights group launches $250K mail campaign targeting Susan Collins
articles.summary: One of the oldest abortion rights groups in the country is launching a $250,000 campaign targeting Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) over her 2018 vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a member of the Supreme Court majority that overturned Roe v. Wade. The direct-mail campaign is being launched by Reproductive Freedom for All (RFFA) and Senate…
articles.body:
One of the oldest abortion rights groups in the country is launching a $250,000 campaign targeting Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) over her 2018 vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a member of the Supreme Court majority that overturned Roe v. Wade.

The direct-mail campaign is being launched by Reproductive Freedom for All (RFFA) and Senate Majority PAC, the main political action committee for Senate Democrats. It will reach more than 100,000 Maine households, targeting women who support reproductive freedom.

Collins is considered one of the most vulnerable Senate Republicans. She is running for reelection for the second time since voting to confirm Kavanaugh, but it’s the first time she has faced voters since Roe was overturned in 2022.

Collins is relying on her reputation as a moderate Republican who supports abortion rights. But the organization’s mailers will accuse her of breaking promises and lying about her vow to protect reproductive rights

The mailers will also highlight Collins’s support for over 100 Trump-appointed judges.

Collins told News Center Maine in a televised interview in June that she does not regret her support for Kavanaugh.

“I do not regret that vote. I do disagree with Justice Kavanaugh’s vote,” Collins said, adding that she was “disappointed” in it.

Kavanaugh was narrowly confirmed by a vote of 50-48, and some Democrats thought at the time that he could have been defeated if Collins had voted no, as that could have swayed then-centrist Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin (W.Va.) to also vote no.

Polls suggest Maine’s longtime senator is running neck-and-neck with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, who has made Collins’s vote for Kavanaugh a centerpiece of his campaign.

The effort is part of RFFA’s $23.5 million midterm campaign to mobilize voters and flip key battleground districts.

“Susan Collins’ lack of leadership and broken promises on reproductive freedom are a glaring vulnerability in this race. She promised to protect her constituents’ fundamental freedoms, and instead helped Donald Trump take them away,” Reproductive Freedom for All President Mini Timmaraju said in a statement.

Timmaraju was in Maine last week to campaign for Jackson after an official endorsement.

The group was one of many Democratic organizations that held back on endorsing a candidate until a successor to former Democratic candidate Graham Platner was established. Now, they are uniting behind Jackson.

“These partisan groups just don’t know what to do about Maine,” said Blake Kernen, a Collins spokesperson. “First, they had to rationalize supporting Graham Platner, who … had to drop out after a rape allegation. Now they are stuck with Troy Jackson.”

Kernen said Collins “has always been pro choice and a champion for Maine women. But because she is a Republican, the national groups continue to twist themselves into a pretzel to support these male candidates with terrible records.”

Kernen also pointed to a 2025 memo from Planned Parenthood referencing Collins’s long support for Medicaid and family planning services, highlighting her opposition to GOP efforts to “defund” the organization.

In August, Planned Parenthood’s political action committee said it was spending more than $600,000 on advertisements attacking Collins for her support of Kavanaugh.

articles.title: Bessent predicts Strait of Hormuz will be ‘worthless’ in 2 years
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday that the Strait of Hormuz will be “worthless” to the oil industry in two years. Speaking to Fox Business’s Larry Kudlow on the sidelines of the Group of 20 finance ministers’ summit in North Carolina, Bessent argued the key waterway is “not a choke point” for the U.S. In…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday that the Strait of Hormuz will be “worthless” to the oil industry in two years.

Speaking to Fox Business’s Larry Kudlow on the sidelines of the Group of 20 finance ministers’ summit in North Carolina, Bessent argued the key waterway is “not a choke point” for the U.S.

In 2024, the country imported roughly half a million barrels of crude oil per day from Persian Gulf countries through the strait, accounting for 7 percent of total U.S. crude oil, according to the Energy Information Administration (EIA).

The analysis from the EIA noted that U.S. crude oil imports from Persian Gulf nations hit their lowest level in nearly 40 years, as “domestic production and imports from Canada have increased.”

Bessent noted the strait is a choke point for “many, many other countries.” Nearly 34 percent of the world’s crude oil passed through the waterway in 2025, per the International Energy Agency (IEA) — which noted “most” of those exports went to Asian countries.

But the Treasury secretary said the strait’s role in the oil trade “will be bypassed” in two years.

“In two years, the Strait of Hormuz will be… a worthless piece of water,” he told Kudlow, adding oil “will be going on pipelines across land.”

The Iranian military’s restrictions on shipping in the strait over six-plus months of war have slowed traffic, resulting in an increase in oil prices.

Brent crude oil, the international benchmark, is trading at more than $95 per barrel as of 3:30 p.m. EDT Wednesday, after closing at $72.48 the day before the U.S. and Israel launched the war in late February.

Gas prices in the U.S. have also spiked, with the national average cost of a gallon of regular gas sitting at $4.09 on Tuesday, according to AAA . Two days before the conflict began, gas in the U.S. cost $2.98 per gallon, AAA reported .

Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) have operational pipelines to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, the IEA notes.

Multiple Middle Eastern governments, including Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iraq and Turkey, have reached agreements with each other to construct oil pipelines . But those pipelines could take multiple years to build, indicating the Strait of Hormuz will remain a key part of the oil trade.

The U.S. military has sought to establish a foothold over the waterway in recent months, guiding tankers through a southern channel of the strait along the coast of Oman and enforcing a monthslong blockade of Iranian ports.

Those moves are part of the Trump administration’s attempts to inflict financial pain on the Islamic Republic, as the Treasury Department ramped up its economic campaign against the regime last week.

The Treasury’s actions included the sanctioning of nearly 60 entities, individuals and vessels that “enable” the Iranian government, with Bessent warning countries to cut financial ties with Iran or risk being cut off from the U.S. dollar system.

On Tuesday, Bessent said the administration has “seen great support” from foreign countries regarding its economic warfare campaign.

“We have zero tolerance,” he told Kudlow. “We are going to economically asphyxiate this regime.”

articles.title: X says attackers are targeting user accounts after the launch of X Money | TechCrunch
articles.summary: X is investigating a wave of unsolicited password reset emails that it believes may be tied to the rollout of its new payments service.
articles.body:
Attackers are attempting to target X users following the launch of X Money. After numerous X users reported receiving unsolicited password reset emails, a representative said the social media company was actively investigating the issue but had not yet found evidence that the hacks were successful.

On Tuesday, X product engineer Mridul Singhai posted to the social network that the company was looking into users’ complaints about the mass password reset attempts.

“Attackers appear to believe that, now that @XMoney is widely available, they can gain unauthorized access to accounts,” he wrote. “We are actively investigating the issue and, so far, have found no evidence of any breaches. We apologize for the multiple emails and appreciate your patience as we work to resolve this.”

X Money is X’s newly launched payments service, which includes a bank card and other benefits. For X, the service could make it easier for creators to collect payments on the platform, further facilitating X’s digital economy.

Of course, money changing hands has a tendency to attract bad actors, which is what X says may be happening here.

X has not posted details to one of its official company accounts as of the time of writing, and has not yet responded to our press inquiry about the matter.

However, X general counsel James Burnham wrote a threatening post, saying, “The legal and security teams @X will stop at nothing to identify, locate, and hold criminally accountable any person anywhere on or off earth who attempts to victimize our platform’s users.”

As the attacks continue, users are warning each other about the problem and reminding others to enable two-factor authentication , if it’s not already enabled, to protect their accounts. X’s chatbot Grok has also replied to some posts with the steps on how to do so, while also confirming that the attackers are “mass-triggering” the form for password resets using public usernames.

“No confirmed system breach or mass takeovers,” the AI bot said.

articles.title: Apple Maps follows Google in renaming Lake Ontario
articles.summary: Apple Maps has changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America following an executive order from President Donald Trump.
articles.body: Apple Maps has officially changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, as reported earlier by Bloomberg. The company joins Google in re-labeling the Great Lake following an executive order signed by President Donald Trump in the midst of a trade dispute with Canada. The Canadian version of Apple Maps still shows “Lake Ontario” when panning over the area, while international versions of the app show both names, according to Bloomberg. Google updated its map shortly after the name change went live in the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), but Apple waited a bit longer. Both Apple and Google changed the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America following a similar executive order signed by Trump last year. Meanwhile, MapQuest refuses to change the name of either body of water, something that has likely helped propel it to the top spot on Apple’s App Store.

articles.title: Hemp ban set to be delayed a month after House passes funding bill
articles.summary: The House on Tuesday passed a short-term government funding bill that will buy the intoxicating hemp industry more time to fight off a looming crackdown on its products. The continuing resolution, which funds the government through Dec. 11, passed in the House on a 370-48 vote — with 19 Republicans and 29 Democrats voting in…
articles.body:
The House on Tuesday passed a short-term government funding bill that will buy the intoxicating hemp industry more time to fight off a looming crackdown on its products.

The continuing resolution, which funds the government through Dec. 11, passed in the House on a 370-48 vote — with 19 Republicans and 29 Democrats voting in opposition. The Senate advanced the measure by a landslide last month, and it now heads to the desk of President Trump.

The measure postpones for a month a federal ban on most hemp-derived THC products, including gummies and beverages.

The provision was inserted into the underlying legislation at the behest of the White House, which has made delaying or otherwise fixing the hemp ban a priority.

Hemp industry groups and their allies are touting Tuesday’s legislation as a significant win that will give them more time to convince lawmakers to regulate their products, rather than ban them.

“This extension gives us one additional month, and we intend to make every day count. We will continue working with lawmakers and stakeholders to advance a comprehensive federal framework that protects consumers, prevents youth access to intoxicating products, provides certainty for farmers and businesses, and preserves access to lawful hemp products,” the U.S. Hemp Roundtable said in an alert to members.

Some hard-line Republicans voted against the continuing resolution — and voted against a rule for four unrelated bills — because of objections to provisions the Senate had added, including the hemp ban delay.

Trump signed the ban into law last year as part of a broader spending bill to reopen the government after a record-long shutdown. It was set to take effect Nov. 12.

The hemp industry has been lobbying furiously against it ever since, arguing the law would collapse a multibillion-dollar industry.

The legislation closed what critics called the “hemp loophole , ” brought about by the 2018 Farm Bill, which removed hemp from the controlled substances list and opened up a massive new business environment.

“The hemp beverage industry looks forward to working with Congress to create a regulatory framework that protects public health, keeps products away from minors, and permanently removes the bad actors that sell untested, high-potency, copycat gummies and candies that target children,” Christopher Lackner, founder and president of the Hemp Beverage Alliance , said in a statement.

But the battle isn’t over, and some Senate and House Republicans have vowed to continue fighting along with representatives of the marijuana industry, which also opposes delaying the ban.

Chris Lindsey, vice president of policy and state advocacy for the American Trade Association for Cannabis and Hemp, said his group is “disappointed” in the delay — even if it was expected.

“Our sights are set on December,” he said. “The loophole empowers bad actors, threatens public health, and undermines state regulations. We urge Congress to end the scourge of ‘gas station weed.’”

articles.title: Hegseth imposes his will on Army with Driscoll resignation
articles.summary: The resignation of Army Secretary Dan Driscoll underlines how Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is increasingly imposing his will on the Pentagon after nearly 20 months in the role. Driscoll’s departure, which came sooner than expected, followed months of tensions with Hegseth, who has forced out or stalled the promotions of dozens of senior military officials…
articles.body:
The resignation of Army Secretary Dan Driscoll underlines how Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is increasingly imposing his will on the Pentagon after nearly 20 months in the role.

Driscoll’s departure, which came sooner than expected, followed months of tensions with Hegseth , who has forced out or stalled the promotions of dozens of senior military officials in a campaign to overhaul the bureaucratic makeup of the Pentagon.

Since arriving at the Pentagon, Hegseth, a former Army National Guard officer, has taken a particular interest in the Army, which now has no Senate-confirmed leader on the civilian or uniformed side of operations.

“He’s absolutely consolidating power and placing loyalists such as General LaNeve into positions such as acting Army chief,” said Kevin Carroll, a retired Army Reserve colonel, referencing Gen. Christopher LaNeve, whom Hegseth slotted as acting Army chief of staff.

Hegseth in April fired Army chief of staff Gen. Randy George, a move that unnerved some Republicans on Capitol Hill.

It left the Army in an “unusual condition,” according to Retired Navy Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery, who added that Driscoll’s resignation is “unfortunate, but expected,” given the secretary’s tangling with Hegseth over George’s removal in early April and the recent retirement of Gen. Chris Donahue, the commander of U.S. Army Europe and Africa .

Army vice chief of staff Gen. James Mingus, who was in the role for less than two years, retired in October without explanation. In his place, President Trump and Hegseth selected LaNeve, Hegseth’s former military adviser.

The Pentagon is pushing to get LaNeve confirmed as Army chief of staff, but he has faced objections from senators on both sides of the aisle.

Montgomery, now a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said Hegseth is forcing unprecedented personnel changes that are leaving the Army weaker.

“I think Hegseth has weakened the Army’s readiness to deal with this significant shortfall, a shortfall that affected the joint forces’ ability to conduct major combat operations against Iran, and would create equal challenges if we had to fight with Russia, China or North Korea,” he told The Hill on Tuesday.

Hegseth is considering his senior adviser and Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell as Driscoll’s successor, The Hill first reported last week . Parnell has been in touch with the White House regarding the possible nomination in recent days, a source familiar with the matter told The Hill on Tuesday.

Carroll, who served in the Office of the Secretary of Defense and on the Joint Staff, argued that Parnell could have a tough time getting confirmed. He pointed to Parnell’s withdrawal from a Senate run in Pennsylvania in 2021 after he lost a court fight over custody of his three children.

Driscoll, a former Army officer and venture capitalist, pushed the Army to modernize equipment, bolster living conditions for service members and have the military learn about drone warfare from Ukrainian forces.

Some of those efforts won bipartisan praise. Among the three service secretaries, Driscoll was doing the best job, a Democratic congressional aide told The Hill in April .

On Tuesday, Democrats and Republicans alike expressed unhappiness with his departure.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), who sits on the Senate Armed Services Committee, told reporters he was “disappointed” to learn of Driscoll’s exit.

“I’m hearing the same rumors everybody else is: that he was frustrated with some of his top generals being released,” Rounds said , adding, “That’s not the first time I’ve heard that.”

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), who sits on the House Armed Services Committee and has criticized Hegseth in the past , said the Constitution gives Hegseth the right to fire three- and four-star military leaders and block promotions, but it does not make it “morally right, and doesn’t make it wise.”

“I think most Americans want more decency, and I would say respect,” Bacon, a retired Air Force brigadier general, said Tuesday during his appearance on CNN. “Respect to say you should give a person a reason why if you’re going to fire them, and that’s not happening here.”

Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said he was “concerned about the Pentagon” and “all of our military.”

“It seems that what they’re doing is anyone who has taken a firm oath of office to support and defend the United States of America their whole career, they’re being … pushed out by a man who was a Fox TV commentator that’s pushed into this position now and does not know, has nowhere near the knowledge and the ability of the general that is pushing out. Not even near,” Meeks told reporters Tuesday.

Meeks added that Hegseth is “the one who should resign.”

Those familiar with Driscoll’s approach to congressional matters argued his bipartisan appeal did not help in his battle for influence with Hegseth.

“One of the things that was an asset during his confirmation may not have been helpful to him in the long run, and that was that he had bipartisan support because he had preexisting relationships,” a former Trump administration official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss Driscoll’s resignation, told The Hill on Tuesday.

Rep. Rich McCormick (R-Ga.), a member of the House Armed Services Committee, waved off concerns about Driscoll’s departure.

“The tactical commanders are much more important as far as the here and the now and our ability to execute warfare on a foreign adversary, so I think we’re in good shape,” he told The Hill. “The Army’s been well prepared.”

McCormick also addressed Hegseth’s decision to block the promotion of four Army officers to one-star rank.

“From what I understand, there was concerns over them being political,” McCormick said. “We serve at the goodwill of the president.”

Hegseth recently blocked the promotion of the four Army officers, some of whom have links to George and Donahue, The Hill previously reported .

“His manipulation of the upcoming one-star list is completely inappropriate and possibly illegal, and I imagine that Driscoll wanted nothing to do with that,” Montgomery said Tuesday.

Other Republican lawmakers expressed their gratitude for Driscoll’s leadership.

Rep. Steve Womack (R-Ark.) lauded the secretary late Monday as “a transformative leader who brought common sense and discipline” to the Army.

Rep. Pat Harrigan (R-N.C.), who sits on the House Armed Services Committee, commended the sense of “urgency” Driscoll brought to his role and noted the secretary’s efforts to modernize the Army.

“From Right to Repair to modernizing acquisition and putting more trust and capability in the hands of soldiers, Dan was willing to take on entrenched systems and challenge assumptions that had gone unquestioned for far too long,” Harrigan wrote late Monday, calling Driscoll “a friend.”
